scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The Grand pas was formalized in the 19th century, most notably through the work of Marius Petipa.
His 1881 revival of the ballet Paquita, with music by Joseph Mazilier, established the Grand Pas Classique as a global standard for ballet companies.
Other historical examples include the 2000 revival of La Fille du pharaon, which adhered to Petipa's original sequence.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The Grand pas serves as a 'pièce de résistance' in a full-length ballet, intended to showcase the technical prowess of the performers.
It is often performed independently of the full ballet.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance follows a specific sequence: an Entrée for the dancers to enter the stage, a Grand adage for the lead ballerina and partner, optional variations for soloists, and a final Coda.
In a Grand pas classique, the focus is on classical technique without character dance or narrative progression.
Watch for Grand adage.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Marius Petipa is the primary choreographer associated with the development and standardization of the Grand pas in the 19th century.
Variants are categorized by the number of dancers: Grand pas de deux (two dancers), Grand pas de trois (three soloists), and Grand pas de quatre (four soloists).
The Grand pas is a core component of classical ballet, evolving from 19th-century court and stage traditions.
